why: GDPR Article 22 limits decisions based only on automated processing. AI Act Article 86 gives people affected by some high-risk AI decisions the right to an explanation.
GDPR Article 15(1)(h) gives people meaningful information about the logic of automated decisions. AI Act Article 86 gives a right to an explanation of the AI system's role in a decision.
GDPR Article 22 is about decisions with no human involved. AI Act Article 14 requires high-risk AI to be built so people can oversee, override and stop it.
AI Act Article 4a lets providers use special categories of personal data (the GDPR Article 9 kind) to find and fix bias, under strict conditions.
GDPR Article 33: report personal data breaches to the regulator. AI Act Article 73: report serious incidents caused by high-risk AI to the market surveillance authority.
Both set the maximum fines and the factors regulators weigh when setting them.
AI Act Article 101 sets the fines for providers of general-purpose AI models; GDPR Article 83 is the GDPR equivalent.
GDPR Article 13 lists what to tell people when collecting their data. AI Act Article 50 requires telling people they are dealing with an AI system or AI-generated content.
GDPR Article 14 lists what to tell people when their data comes from somewhere else. AI Act Article 50 requires telling people they are dealing with an AI system or AI-generated content.
GDPR Article 5 requires data to be accurate, relevant and limited to what is needed. AI Act Article 10 sets quality rules for the data used to train and test high-risk AI.
GDPR Article 25 requires data protection by design. AI Act Article 9 requires a risk management system across the whole life of a high-risk AI system.
GDPR Article 30 requires records of processing activities. AI Act Article 12 requires high-risk AI to keep automatic logs. Different records, same idea of being able to show what happened.
GDPR Article 32 requires security of processing. AI Act Article 15 requires high-risk AI to be accurate, robust and secure.
Under AI Act Article 74(8), data protection authorities are the market surveillance authorities for some high-risk AI systems, for example in law enforcement, migration and justice.
Both give people the right to complain to a regulator: a data protection authority under the GDPR, a market surveillance authority under the AI Act.
Both reach organisations outside the EU when what they do targets or affects people in the EU.
AI Act Article 59 lets personal data collected for other purposes be used to develop some public-interest AI systems in a regulatory sandbox. GDPR Article 6(4) covers using data for a new purpose.
Both encourage voluntary codes of conduct that help organisations apply the rules.
The European Data Protection Board (GDPR) and the European AI Board (AI Act) both bring the national regulators together at EU level.
